name: REST
what: Resource-oriented design where nouns are addressed by URLs and manipulated with a uniform set of HTTP methods.
when: You are exposing business entities to a broad, unknown set of consumers.
watch: Purist debates about "true REST" distract from consistency, which is what consumers actually need.

name: Hypermedia (HATEOAS)
what: Responses carry links and actions that tell the client what it can do next, so clients follow links instead of building URLs.
when: Workflows change often and you want clients to discover state transitions at runtime.
watch: Few client libraries consume hypermedia generically; most consumers hard-code URLs anyway.

name: RPC over HTTP
what: Expose procedures (verbs) instead of resources, typically POSTing a method name and arguments.
when: The domain is action-heavy and does not map cleanly onto resources.
watch: Loses HTTP caching and method semantics; every call looks like a POST.

name: JSON-RPC
what: A lightweight, transport-agnostic RPC envelope with id, method, params, and result/error.
when: You want simple RPC over HTTP, WebSocket, or raw TCP with batching built in.
watch: No schema or discovery story on its own; the MCP protocol now builds on it.

name: gRPC
what: Contract-first RPC using Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, supporting unary and streaming calls.
when: Internal service-to-service traffic where performance, typed contracts and streaming matter.
watch: Browsers need gRPC-Web or Connect, and the binary payloads are harder to debug by eye.

name: gRPC-Web / Connect
what: Browser- and HTTP/1.1-friendly variants of gRPC that keep protobuf contracts but work through ordinary proxies.
when: You want one protobuf contract serving both backend and browser clients.
watch: Client streaming support is limited in browsers.

name: GraphQL
what: A typed schema with a query language that lets clients ask for exactly the fields they need in one round trip.
when: Many client types with different data needs over a connected graph of entities.
watch: HTTP caching is harder, query cost must be limited, and errors come back with 200 status codes.
refs: GraphQL spec, GraphQL over HTTP, apis.io GraphQL

name: GraphQL Federation
what: Compose many team-owned GraphQL subgraphs into a single supergraph behind a router.
when: Several teams own parts of one graph and need to ship independently.
watch: Adds a router tier and cross-team schema governance.
refs: Apollo Federation, GraphQL Composite Schemas WG

name: SOAP
what: XML envelope protocol with a WSDL contract and the WS-* extensions for security and transactions.
when: Integrating with enterprise, government, or financial systems that already speak it.
watch: Verbose and heavyweight; a poor choice for new public APIs.

name: OData
what: A REST convention with a standardized query language ($filter, $select, $expand) and metadata documents.
when: Data-centric APIs consumed by analytics and BI tooling.
watch: Lets clients compose expensive queries, and the URLs get unwieldy.

name: Backend for Frontend (BFF)
what: A dedicated API layer per client experience (web, mobile, partner) that tailors and aggregates downstream services.
when: Different clients need very different shapes and cadences.
watch: Duplicated logic across BFFs; ownership can drift.

name: API Gateway
what: A single entry point that handles routing, auth, rate limiting, transformation and observability for many backends.
when: You run more than a handful of APIs and want consistent policy enforcement.
watch: Becomes a bottleneck or a dumping ground for business logic.
example: Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway, Envoy

name: API Composition / Aggregation
what: One endpoint calls several services and merges the results so clients make one call instead of many.
when: Chatty clients are paying latency for many sequential calls.
watch: Partial failures need a policy: fail the whole response or degrade.

name: Façade
what: A simplified, stable interface placed in front of a complex or legacy system.
when: Modernizing a legacy system without forcing consumers to change.
watch: The façade can leak legacy semantics if you only rename things.

name: Anti-Corruption Layer
what: A translation layer that keeps a foreign model from leaking into your domain.
when: Integrating with a third-party or legacy API whose model you do not want to adopt.
watch: Extra mapping code to maintain.
example: Adapter mapping a vendor's "Client" into your "Customer"

name: Strangler Fig
what: Incrementally route endpoints from a legacy system to a new one behind the same interface.
when: Replacing a monolith or old API without a big-bang cutover.
watch: Running two systems for a long time.
example: Gateway routes /orders/* to the new service, everything else to legacy

name: Event-Driven API
what: Expose state changes as events that consumers subscribe to rather than poll for.
when: Consumers need to react to changes quickly and at scale.
watch: Ordering, delivery guarantees and replay need careful design.

name: CQRS
what: Separate the write (command) model and API from the read (query) model and API.
when: Read and write workloads have very different shapes or scale.
watch: Eventual consistency between the two sides surprises consumers.

name: Collection / Item Resources
what: Plural collection URLs list and create; item URLs address one member by id.
watch: Inconsistent pluralization across an API erodes trust.

name: Sub-Resources / Nesting
what: Express ownership by nesting child collections under a parent.
when: The child cannot exist without the parent.
watch: Deep nesting (more than two levels) makes URLs brittle.

name: Singleton Resource
what: A resource with exactly one instance per parent or caller, addressed without an id.
watch: It cannot be created or deleted the way a collection item can.

name: Controller / Action Resource
what: Model an operation that does not fit CRUD as a verb sub-resource, invoked with POST.
when: State transitions such as cancel, approve, or refund.
watch: Overuse turns REST back into RPC.

name: Custom Methods
what: Colon-suffixed verbs on a resource or collection for non-standard operations.
when: You want explicit verbs without inventing sub-resources.
watch: Some routers and proxies mishandle colons in paths.

name: Lookup by Alternate Key
what: Address a resource by a natural or business key as well as its id.
when: Consumers know the email or SKU but not your internal id.
watch: Two URLs for the same thing complicates caching and canonical links.

name: Search Endpoint
what: A dedicated search resource, often POST, accepting a rich query body.
when: Queries are too complex or too long for a query string.
watch: POST search loses cacheability (HTTP QUERY addresses this).

name: HTTP QUERY Method
what: A safe, idempotent method that carries a request body, so searches can be cached and retried like GET.
when: Complex read queries that need a body without the semantics of POST.
watch: Still a draft; gateway and client support is thin.

name: Bulk / Batch Operations
what: Create, update or delete many resources in one request.
when: Imports, syncs, and anything that would otherwise take thousands of calls.
watch: Partial failure reporting and payload size limits.

name: Composite Request
what: Send several dependent sub-requests in one envelope, referencing earlier results.
when: Mobile or low-bandwidth clients that need transactional multi-step writes.
watch: Complex to implement and to document.

name: Long-Running Operation Resource
what: Return an operation resource that the client polls until the work is done.
when: Work that takes longer than a reasonable request timeout.
watch: Clients must implement polling and handle expiry.

name: Polymorphic Resources
what: One endpoint returns several subtypes, distinguished by a discriminator field.
when: Payment methods, notifications and other naturally variant types.
watch: Code generators handle oneOf and discriminators unevenly.

name: Resource Expansion
what: Let clients ask for related objects to be embedded inline instead of returned as ids.
when: Clients routinely make follow-up calls to fetch related objects.
watch: Unbounded expansion creates expensive responses.

name: Sparse Fieldsets
what: Clients choose which fields come back.
watch: Responses vary per request, which complicates caching.
refs: JSON:API sparse fieldsets, Google field masks

name: Views / Projections
what: Named response shapes (basic, full) instead of arbitrary field selection.
when: You want controlled payload sizes without open-ended selection.
watch: Only works if you pick a few views and stick to them.

name: Filtering
what: Narrow a collection by field values through query parameters or a filter expression.
watch: Ad-hoc filter syntaxes differ in every API.

name: Sorting
what: Let the client order results by one or more fields.
watch: Sorting on unindexed fields hurts at scale.

name: Offset Pagination
what: Page with offset and limit (or page and per_page).
when: Small or static datasets where jumping to page N matters.
watch: Slow on large tables, and it skips or duplicates rows as data changes.

name: Cursor Pagination
what: Return an opaque cursor that points at the next page.
when: Large or fast-changing datasets and feeds.
watch: There is no random access to page N.

name: Keyset Pagination
what: Paginate with a WHERE clause on the last seen sort key instead of an offset.
when: Very large tables that need stable, fast paging.
watch: Needs a unique, indexed sort key.

name: Link Header Pagination
what: Advertise next, prev, first and last pages in the HTTP Link header.
when: You want pagination that stays out of the response body.
watch: Easy for clients to miss; some proxies strip headers.

name: Total Count
what: Report the total number of matching items alongside a page.
when: UIs need page counts or progress.
watch: Exact counts are expensive on large datasets, so consider estimates.

name: Full-Text Search Parameter
what: A single q parameter for relevance-ranked text search.
watch: Ranking is opaque to consumers.

name: Faceting / Aggregations
what: Return counts grouped by field values with the results.
when: Search UIs with filter sidebars, and analytics.
watch: Expensive to compute; cache the facet counts.

name: Idempotency Keys
what: The client sends a unique key so the server can safely deduplicate retried POSTs.
when: Payments and anything else where a duplicate write is costly.
watch: Keys need storage, expiry and request-fingerprint matching.

name: Idempotent Methods
what: PUT and DELETE produce the same result however many times they are applied.
when: Designing writes that are safe to retry.
watch: Side effects such as emails break the guarantee.

name: PUT Full Replace
what: Replace the whole resource representation.
watch: Missing fields get wiped, which surprises clients.

name: JSON Merge Patch
what: PATCH with a partial document; null deletes a field.
watch: You cannot set a value to null, and arrays are replaced wholesale.

name: JSON Patch
what: PATCH with an ordered list of operations (add, remove, replace, move, test).
when: Precise array edits and conditional updates.
watch: Verbose, and hard for humans to write.

name: Field Masks
what: An explicit list of the fields an update touches.
when: Partial updates that need unambiguous semantics.
watch: One more parameter to keep in sync with the body.

name: Upsert
what: Create the resource if it is missing, update it if it exists, usually through PUT to a client-chosen id.
when: Syncing from systems that own their own ids.
watch: Typos silently create new records.

name: Optimistic Concurrency
what: Writes include the version the client last saw and are rejected if it changed.
when: Concurrent editors could overwrite each other (lost updates).
watch: Clients must handle 412 and retry or merge.

name: Soft Delete
what: Mark resources deleted and hide them instead of destroying them.
watch: Uniqueness constraints and "show deleted" filters get tricky.

name: Undelete / Restore
what: An explicit operation to bring back a soft-deleted resource.
watch: Define how long a resource stays recoverable.

name: Partial Success (207)
what: Report per-item results for a batch instead of a single status.
when: Bulk operations where some items fail.
watch: Clients treat the 2xx as total success unless they look inside.

name: Client-Generated IDs
what: The client chooses the id at creation time.
watch: Collisions and enumeration need validation.

name: State Machine Transitions
what: Model lifecycle states explicitly and only allow valid transitions.
when: Orders, tickets, approvals and other workflow-heavy domains.
watch: Clients need the state diagram, so document it.

name: Asynchronous Request-Reply (202)
what: Accept work with 202 and a Location for a status resource the client polls.
watch: Polling cost, plus cleanup of finished status resources.

name: Polling
what: The client repeatedly asks for changes or status.
watch: Wasted calls and added latency; send Retry-After hints.

name: Long Polling
what: The server holds a request open until there is data or a timeout, then the client re-requests.
watch: Ties up connections, and proxies may cut long requests.

name: Webhooks
what: The provider POSTs an event to a URL the consumer registered.
when: Consumers need push notifications of changes.
watch: Delivery retries, ordering, security and consumer downtime.

name: Signed Webhooks
what: Sign webhook payloads (HMAC or asymmetric) so consumers can verify their origin.
watch: Clock skew and replay; include timestamps.

name: Webhook Subscription Management
what: An API to create, list, test and delete webhook subscriptions.
watch: Validate the endpoint first (challenge-response).

name: Thin Events / Fetch-Back
what: Events carry only ids and the consumer fetches the current state.
when: Payloads are sensitive or out-of-order delivery is common.
watch: Doubles the call volume.

name: Event-Carried State Transfer
what: Events carry the full changed state so consumers never call back.
when: Decoupled consumers that keep their own copies.
watch: Large payloads and schema evolution.

name: Callbacks
what: The request includes a URL where the result will be POSTed when ready.
when: A one-off async result for a single request.
watch: Same delivery problems as webhooks.

name: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
what: A one-way server-to-client stream of text events over a plain HTTP response.
when: Live feeds, progress and LLM token streaming.
watch: One direction only; connection limits apply on HTTP/1.1.

name: WebSockets
what: A full-duplex, message-oriented connection upgraded from HTTP and running over TCP.
watch: Stateful connections complicate scaling, auth refresh and load balancing.

name: HTTP Streaming / NDJSON
what: Stream a large or unbounded response as newline-delimited records.
watch: Errors that happen mid-stream need an in-band signal.

name: WebSub
what: Hub-based publish/subscribe for web content using webhooks.
watch: Few new adopters.

name: Streamable HTTP (MCP)
what: A single endpoint that answers JSON-RPC POSTs with JSON or upgrades the response to an SSE stream.
when: Agent tool servers that need both request-response and streaming.
watch: Session management and resumability are still settling.

name: Webhook Retry with Backoff
what: Retry failed deliveries on an increasing schedule, then dead-letter them.
watch: Duplicate deliveries mean consumers must be idempotent.

name: Event Replay / Redelivery
what: Let consumers re-fetch or replay missed events from a log or an events endpoint.
watch: Requires retention and cursors.

name: Content Negotiation
what: The client states preferred formats and the server picks one.
when: Several representations of the same resource (JSON, CSV, XML).
watch: Vary headers are needed for correct caching.

name: Media Type Design
what: Define custom or profiled media types that carry semantics and version.
when: Hypermedia, or versioning through media types.
watch: Tooling rarely understands custom types.

name: Envelope vs Bare Responses
what: Wrap payloads in a data/meta/links envelope, or return the resource directly.
when: Envelopes help with pagination metadata; bare bodies are simpler.
watch: Mixing the two styles in one API.

name: Problem Details
what: A standard JSON error format with type, title, status, detail and instance.
watch: Teams invent their own extensions inconsistently.

name: Consistent Error Codes
what: Stable, machine-readable error codes alongside human messages.
watch: Codes multiply without a registry.

name: Status Code Semantics
what: Use the right status class and code (201, 204, 400, 404, 409, 422, 429, 503).
watch: Returning 200 with an error body defeats tooling.

name: Standard Date / Money / Locale Formats
what: ISO 8601 timestamps, ISO 4217 currencies, minor-unit integers, and BCP 47 languages.
when: Any API with times, money or text.
watch: Floats for money; local times without an offset.

name: Enumerations with Unknowns
what: Treat enums as open: clients must tolerate values they have not seen.
watch: Strict generated clients crash on new values.

name: Null vs Absent
what: Define clearly whether a missing field and a null field mean different things.
watch: Ambiguity causes accidental data wipes.

name: Opaque Identifiers
what: Ids are strings with no meaning clients should parse, often type-prefixed.
when: Always; it keeps you free to change storage.
watch: Clients still parse them if you leak structure.

name: Hypermedia Links in Payloads
what: Include self and related links in responses.
when: You want discoverability and fewer client-built URLs.
watch: Payload bloat if the links are not used.

name: Localization
what: Return translated content based on Accept-Language.
watch: Caching needs Vary: Accept-Language.

name: Binary / File Upload (Multipart)
what: Send files and metadata together in a multipart/form-data request.
watch: Memory pressure on large files.

name: Presigned / Direct Upload URLs
what: The API returns a short-lived URL so clients upload straight to object storage.
when: Large files that should not pass through your servers.
watch: Expiry and validation happen out of band.

name: Resumable Uploads
what: Upload in chunks that can resume after interruption.
watch: Server-side state for incomplete uploads.

name: Range Requests
what: Fetch part of a resource by byte range.
watch: Rarely implemented on dynamic resources.

name: URI Versioning
what: Put the major version in the path.
when: Public APIs that need simple, visible versioning.
watch: Every version is a new API to maintain.

name: Header / Media Type Versioning
what: Select the version with a header or an Accept parameter.
when: You want stable URLs for resources.
watch: Harder to test in a browser, and easy to forget.

name: Date-Based Versioning
what: Pin each consumer to the API as it was on a date, with server-side transforms.
when: Many small, frequent changes without breaking anyone.
watch: The transform layer is real engineering.

name: Query Parameter Versioning
what: The version is chosen through a query parameter.
watch: Pollutes cache keys and is easy to omit.

name: Additive-Only Change
what: Evolve by adding fields and endpoints, never removing or repurposing them.
watch: Accumulated cruft.

name: Tolerant Reader
what: Clients ignore unknown fields and depend only on what they need.
watch: Strict deserializers break it.

name: Deprecation Header
what: Signal in responses that an endpoint is deprecated.
watch: Nobody reads headers unless tools surface them.

name: Sunset Header
what: Announce when an endpoint will stop working.
watch: You have to actually honor the date.

name: Consumer-Driven Contracts
what: Consumers publish their expectations as tests the provider runs.
when: Many internal consumers of an evolving API.
watch: Contract tests are extra infrastructure.
example: Pact contract files verified in provider CI

name: Feature Flags / Previews
what: Opt-in headers or flags for beta behavior.
watch: Previews that never graduate.

name: Expand / Contract Migration
what: Add the new shape, migrate consumers, then remove the old one.
when: Breaking changes in schemas or databases.
watch: It takes discipline to finish the contract step.

name: API Keys
what: A static secret identifying the calling application.
watch: Not user identity; leaked keys are common.

name: OAuth 2.x Authorization Code + PKCE
what: Delegated user authorization through a browser redirect.
when: Third-party apps acting on behalf of users.
watch: Complex for beginners; requires redirect handling.
refs: RFC 6749, RFC 7636, OAuth 2.1 draft, apis.io Security

name: OAuth Client Credentials
what: Machine-to-machine tokens without a user.
watch: Over-broad scopes.

name: Device Authorization Grant
what: Users authorize on another device with a code.
watch: Polling the token endpoint.

name: Token Exchange
what: Swap one token for another with a different audience or scope.
watch: Tracking who acted on behalf of whom.

name: OpenID Connect
what: An identity layer on OAuth that returns an ID token about the user.
watch: Do not use ID tokens as API access tokens.

name: JWT Bearer Tokens
what: Self-contained signed tokens validated without a lookup.
watch: Revocation is hard, so keep them short-lived.

name: Scopes and Fine-Grained Permissions
what: Tokens carry narrow scopes or rich authorization details.
when: Least privilege for apps and agents.
watch: Scope explosion.
refs: RFC 9396 Rich Authorization Requests, apis.io Scopes

name: mTLS
what: Both client and server present certificates.
when: Zero-trust service meshes and financial APIs.
watch: Certificate lifecycle operations.
example: Client cert bound to the access token

name: HMAC Request Signing
what: Sign the request (method, path, body, timestamp) with a shared secret.
when: Tamper-proof requests without TLS termination trust.
watch: Canonicalization bugs.

name: HTTP Message Signatures
what: A standard for signing selected HTTP message components.
when: Interoperable request and response signing, including agent identity.
watch: Young ecosystem.

name: DPoP
what: Sender-constrained tokens bound to a client key so stolen tokens are useless.
when: Public clients where token theft is a risk.
watch: Extra proof JWT on every call.

name: CORS
what: Browser rules for which origins may call your API.
when: Any API called from browser JavaScript.
watch: A wildcard origin combined with credentials.

name: Multi-Tenancy Addressing
what: Identify the tenant by subdomain, path, header or token claim.
watch: Per-tenant hosts break discovery.

name: Rate Limiting
what: Cap requests per client per window and reject the excess with 429.
watch: Opaque limits frustrate developers, so publish them.
refs: RFC 6585, IETF RateLimit headers draft, apis.io Rate Limits

name: RateLimit Headers
what: Tell clients their quota and what remains on every response.
watch: Header names vary across providers until the draft settles.

name: Quotas and Usage Plans
what: Daily or monthly allowances tied to a plan or tier.
watch: Hard cut-offs mid-month anger customers.
refs: API gateway usage plans, apis.io Plans

name: Token Bucket / Leaky Bucket
what: Algorithms that allow bursts while enforcing an average rate.
watch: Distributed counters across nodes.

name: Retry-After
what: Tell clients when to try again after a 429 or 503.
watch: Clients that ignore it.

name: Load Shedding
what: Deliberately reject low-priority work under overload.
watch: Choosing what to shed.

name: Priority Queues / Fair Queuing
what: Isolate tenants or request classes so one cannot starve the others.
watch: Configuration complexity.

name: HTTP Caching (Cache-Control)
what: Tell clients and CDNs how long a response is fresh.
watch: Caching personalized data publicly.

name: ETag / Conditional GET
what: Validators let clients revalidate and receive 304 Not Modified.
watch: Weak vs strong ETag semantics.

name: stale-while-revalidate
what: Serve stale content while refreshing in the background.
watch: Consumers briefly see old data.

name: CDN / Edge APIs
what: Serve or compute API responses at edge locations.
when: Global audiences and static catalog data.
watch: Invalidation and consistency.

name: Compression
what: gzip, br or zstd response bodies.
when: JSON payloads over a few KB.
watch: CPU cost; BREACH with secrets in the body.

name: HTTP/2 Multiplexing
what: Many concurrent streams over one TCP connection.
watch: TCP head-of-line blocking still applies.

name: HTTP/3 / QUIC
what: HTTP over QUIC (UDP), with independent streams and 0-RTT resumption.
watch: UDP blocked on some enterprise networks.

name: Request Coalescing
what: Collapse identical in-flight requests into one backend call.
watch: Adds latency to the first request.

name: Prefer Header
what: Clients state preferences such as return=minimal or respond-async.
when: Letting clients trade payload size or sync behavior.
watch: Servers may ignore it; signal with Preference-Applied.

name: Delta / Changes Feed
what: Return only what changed since a token.
watch: Token expiry and full-resync fallback.

name: Retries with Backoff and Jitter
what: Retry transient failures with exponentially growing, randomized delays.
when: Every client of every network API.
watch: Retrying non-idempotent calls without idempotency keys.

name: Timeouts and Deadlines
what: Every call has a time budget, propagated downstream.
watch: Missing timeouts cause cascading hangs.

name: Circuit Breaker
what: Stop calling a failing dependency for a while and fail fast.
when: Protecting callers from slow or dead services.
watch: Tuning thresholds.

name: Bulkhead
what: Isolate resources so one failing dependency cannot exhaust them all.
when: Services that depend on many backends.
watch: Underused pools.

name: Fallback / Graceful Degradation
what: Return cached, default or partial data when a dependency fails.
watch: Silent degradation hides outages.

name: Hedged Requests
what: Send a duplicate request after a delay and take whichever answers first.
watch: Extra load; only for idempotent reads.
example: Backup request after the p95 delay

name: Health Check Endpoints
what: Liveness and readiness endpoints for orchestrators and monitors.
when: Anything deployed behind a load balancer.
watch: Deep checks that cascade failures.
refs: IETF Health Check Response Format draft

name: Correlation / Trace IDs
what: Propagate a request id through every hop for debugging and tracing.
watch: Not echoing the id back to the client.

name: Request IDs in Responses
what: Return a unique id clients can quote to support.
watch: Logs not indexed by the id.

name: Structured Audit Logs
what: Record who did what and when, as data consumers can query.
watch: Logging PII.

name: Usage / Analytics API
what: Expose consumers' own usage, errors and latency to them.
watch: Data freshness.

name: Status Page / Incident API
what: A machine-readable service status.
watch: Keeping it honest.

name: OpenAPI Description
what: A machine-readable contract for an HTTP API.
when: Every HTTP API, for docs, SDKs, testing, governance and agents.
watch: Contracts that drift from the implementation.

name: AsyncAPI Description
what: A machine-readable contract for event-driven and message APIs.
when: Kafka, MQTT, WebSocket and webhook APIs.
watch: Less tooling than OpenAPI.

name: Arazzo Workflows
what: Describe multi-step sequences of API calls and their dependencies.
when: Documenting real use cases and powering agents.
watch: Young tooling.

name: Overlays
what: Apply repeatable changes to an OpenAPI document without editing the source.
watch: Yet another file to keep in sync.

name: Protocol Buffers / IDL Contracts
what: Interface definition languages that generate code for both ends.
watch: Coordinating schema changes.

name: JSON Schema
what: A vocabulary for validating and describing JSON payloads.
watch: Dialect differences across tools.

name: Schema Registry
what: A central store of versioned message schemas with compatibility checks.
watch: An operational dependency.

name: APIs.json
what: A machine-readable index of a provider's APIs and their supporting resources.
watch: Needs to be kept current.

name: Well-Known URIs
what: Predictable /.well-known/ paths for metadata.
when: OAuth metadata, API catalogs and agent cards.
watch: Registered names only.

name: OAuth Server Metadata
what: Publish authorization server endpoints and capabilities.
watch: Forgetting protected-resource metadata.

name: llms.txt
what: A Markdown index of docs written for LLMs.
when: Helping AI assistants find your docs.
watch: Not a contract; it is guidance only.

name: MCP Server
what: Expose API capabilities as tools, resources and prompts that AI agents can call.
when: Making an API usable by agents.
watch: Auth, tool sprawl and per-tenant discovery.

name: Agent Cards (A2A)
what: A JSON card describing an agent's skills and endpoints for agent-to-agent calls.
when: Publishing an agent rather than an API.
watch: Early standard.

name: SDK Generation
what: Generate typed client libraries from the contract.
when: Lowering the integration cost across languages.
watch: Generated code quality varies.

name: Sandbox / Test Mode
what: A safe environment with test credentials and fake data.
when: Payments and anything with real-world side effects.
watch: Sandboxes that drift from production behavior.

name: Mock Servers
what: Serve example responses from the contract before the backend exists.
watch: Mocks that lie about behavior.

name: Interactive Docs / Try It
what: Docs that make live calls.
watch: Exposing production keys.

name: Self-Service Onboarding
what: Sign up, get a key and make a first call with no humans involved.
watch: Abuse and fraud.

name: Changelog / Release Notes
what: A dated, machine-readable record of API changes.
watch: Changelogs that skip breaking changes.

name: Request/Response Examples
what: Concrete examples for every operation in docs and contracts.
when: Always; they are how most people learn.
watch: Examples that are invalid against the schema.

name: Request / Response (Synchronous RPC)
what: The client sends a message on a connection and blocks for the matching reply.
watch: Head-of-line blocking without pipelining.

name: Fire-and-Forget (One-Way)
what: Send a message with no reply expected.
watch: Silent loss.

name: Publish / Subscribe
what: Publishers send to topics; brokers fan messages out to subscribers.
watch: Delivery guarantees vary by broker.
refs: MQTT, AMQP, NATS, Kafka, apis.io Channels

name: Point-to-Point Queue
what: Each message is consumed by exactly one worker from a queue.
watch: Poison messages; use dead-letter queues.

name: Competing Consumers
what: Several workers read from one queue to scale processing.
watch: Ordering is lost.
example: N workers on one SQS queue

name: Request-Reply over Messaging
what: Send a request with a reply-to address and a correlation id over a broker.
watch: Timeout and orphaned-reply handling.

name: Push / Pull Pipeline
what: Distribute tasks downstream and collect results upstream.
watch: No broker-level persistence.

name: Dealer / Router
what: Asynchronous, addressable request-reply for brokers and load balancers.
watch: Complex to reason about.

name: Fan-Out / Fan-In
what: Split work across many recipients, then aggregate the results.
watch: Waiting on the slowest participant.

name: Bidirectional Streaming
what: Both sides send independent message streams over one connection.
watch: Flow control and error handling.

name: Server Push Stream
what: The server pushes updates on an open connection after one subscribe.
watch: Reconnect and resubscribe logic.

name: Event Log / Append-Only Stream
what: Consumers read an ordered, replayable log at their own offsets.
when: Event sourcing, CDC and analytics pipelines.
watch: Retention and partition design.

name: Dead Letter Queue
what: Route messages that repeatedly fail into a side queue for inspection.
watch: DLQs nobody watches.

name: Message Ordering Keys
what: Guarantee order per key (partition) rather than globally.
watch: Hot keys.

name: Exactly-Once / Effectively-Once
what: Idempotent producers plus transactional consumption to avoid duplicates.
watch: Narrow guarantees and real cost.

name: Length-Prefixed Framing
what: Each message begins with its byte length.
watch: Max-length checks against hostile peers.

name: Delimiter-Based Framing
what: Messages end with a delimiter such as CRLF or a newline.
when: Text protocols that people can debug with telnet.
watch: Escaping delimiters inside payloads.
example: SMTP, Redis RESP, NDJSON over TCP

name: Fixed-Length Records
what: Every message is exactly N bytes.
watch: Wasted space, rigid evolution.

name: Type-Length-Value (TLV)
what: Fields are encoded as type, length and value, so unknown fields can be skipped.
watch: Parsing overhead.

name: Protocol Buffers Encoding
what: Compact, tagged binary encoding with forward and backward compatibility.
watch: Not self-describing without the schema.

name: Avro / Thrift / Cap'n Proto
what: Alternative schema-based binary encodings with different evolution and zero-copy tradeoffs.
watch: Ecosystem lock-in.
refs: Apache Avro, Apache Thrift, Cap'n Proto

name: MessagePack / CBOR
what: Schemaless binary JSON-like encodings.
when: You want JSON semantics with smaller, faster payloads.
watch: Harder to inspect than JSON.

name: Multiplexed Streams over One Connection
what: Frames carry stream ids so many logical conversations share one socket.
watch: One slow stream can starve others without flow control.
example: HTTP/2 stream id, yamux, SSH channels

name: Pipelining
what: Send several requests without waiting for replies, which come back in order.
when: Cutting round trips on high-latency links.
watch: Head-of-line blocking.

name: Correlation IDs for Out-of-Order Replies
what: Tag each request so responses can arrive in any order.
watch: Unbounded tables of outstanding requests.

name: Handshake / Capability Negotiation
what: Peers exchange versions and features before real traffic.
when: Evolving protocols with mixed client versions.
watch: Downgrade attacks.
example: TLS ClientHello, MCP initialize, AMQP Connection.Start

name: Persistent Connections / Keep-Alive
what: Reuse one connection for many requests.
watch: Idle connections killed by NATs and load balancers.

name: Connection Pooling
what: Clients keep a pool of warm connections.
when: High-throughput clients of databases and services.
watch: Pool exhaustion and stale connections.

name: Heartbeats / Ping-Pong
what: Periodic frames prove the peer is alive and keep NAT mappings open.
watch: Choosing intervals and timeouts.
example: WebSocket ping, MQTT PINGREQ, AMQP heartbeat

name: Reconnect with Backoff
what: Clients reconnect automatically after drops with increasing delays.
watch: Thundering herds after an outage; add jitter.

name: Session Resumption
what: Resume a session's state or position after reconnecting.
watch: Server-side session storage.
example: MQTT clean_session=false, TLS session tickets, SSE Last-Event-ID

name: Graceful Shutdown / Draining
what: Tell peers to stop opening new streams and finish in-flight work.
watch: Clients that ignore the signal.

name: Stateful Session vs Stateless
what: Decide whether a connection carries context (auth, transactions) or each message stands alone.
watch: Stateful sessions complicate load balancing and failover.

name: SASL Authentication Exchange
what: A pluggable challenge-response auth step at connection time.
watch: Mechanism negotiation complexity.

name: TLS / mTLS on Raw Sockets
what: Encrypt and authenticate TCP streams.
when: Every protocol on an untrusted network.
watch: Certificate rotation.

name: Backpressure
what: Slow receivers signal senders to slow down instead of buffering unbounded data.
when: Streams where the producer can outpace the consumer.
watch: Ignoring it leads to memory blow-ups.

name: Credit-Based Flow Control / Windowing
what: Receivers grant credits or windows for how much may be sent.
watch: Window tuning.

name: Acknowledgements (Ack / Nack)
what: Consumers confirm processing so brokers can redeliver failed messages.
watch: Acking before processing loses messages.

name: Delivery Guarantees (QoS Levels)
what: Choose at-most-once, at-least-once or exactly-once per message.
watch: Higher guarantees cost latency.

name: Sequence Numbers and Replay
what: Number messages so gaps and duplicates can be detected and replayed.
when: Market data feeds and sync protocols.
watch: Retention windows.

name: Batching and Nagle Tuning
what: Group small writes for throughput, or disable Nagle for latency.
watch: Delayed ACK interaction.

name: Snapshot + Incremental Updates
what: Send the full state first, then deltas, resyncing on gaps.
when: Order books, collaborative docs and caches.
watch: Snapshot cost.
example: Exchange L2 book snapshot then diffs

name: Request Queueing / Admission Control
what: Bound the number of in-flight requests and queue or reject the excess.
watch: Queue-induced latency.

name: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing
what: Balance by connection (TCP) or by request (HTTP).
when: Long-lived connections need L7 or client-side balancing.
watch: L4 balancing pins gRPC streams to a single backend.

name: Client-Side Load Balancing
what: Clients discover endpoints and balance across them directly.
watch: Clients need service discovery.

name: Service Discovery
what: Look up service endpoints dynamically.
watch: Stale registrations.

name: Sidecar / Service Mesh
what: A proxy beside each service handles mTLS, retries and telemetry.
when: Uniform cross-cutting policy across many services.
watch: Operational weight.

name: Sticky Sessions
what: Route a client consistently to the same backend.
watch: Uneven load and painful failover.

name: Reverse Proxy
what: An intermediary terminates client connections and forwards them to backends.
watch: Header and timeout mismatches.

name: Reactor / Event Loop Server
what: One thread multiplexes many non-blocking sockets.
watch: Blocking calls freeze everything.

name: Thread-per-Connection
what: Each connection gets a dedicated thread.
watch: Memory and context-switch cost at scale.

name: Broker vs Brokerless
what: Route messages through a central broker, or peer-to-peer.
watch: A broker is a dependency; brokerless pushes complexity into clients.

name: Tunneling over HTTP
what: Carry TCP or UDP traffic through HTTP CONNECT or MASQUE.
watch: Visibility and security review.

name: Agent Tool Calling
what: Describe operations so LLMs can choose and invoke them with structured arguments.
watch: Vague descriptions mean the wrong tool gets picked.

name: Natural-Language Operation Descriptions
what: Write operation summaries and descriptions for machine reasoning, not just humans.
when: Agents and search will consume your contract.
watch: Marketing-speak descriptions.
example: summary: "Refund a captured charge, fully or partially"

name: Agent-Readable Errors
what: Errors explain what to change and point to the fix, so agents can self-correct.
watch: Leaking internals.
example: {"detail":"amount must be <= 5000; split into two calls"}

name: Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation
what: Destructive or costly operations require explicit confirmation or elicitation.
watch: Prompt fatigue.

name: Scoped Agent Credentials
what: Short-lived, narrowly scoped, auditable tokens issued to agents.
when: Letting agents act without full user power.
watch: Delegation chains are hard to audit.
example: Token exchange with an actor claim

name: Agent-to-Agent Messaging
what: Agents discover and delegate tasks to each other through published cards and task APIs.
watch: Trust and identity are unresolved.

name: Free Tier
what: A no-cost plan with limited volume or features, so developers can build before they buy.
when: Developer-led adoption, where the first call should never need a credit card.
watch: A free tier that is too small to prove value, or so generous nobody upgrades.

name: Freemium to Paid Tiers
what: Good/better/best plans that bundle quotas, features and support levels.
when: Serving hobbyists through to enterprises with one product.
watch: Too many tiers; feature gating that blocks evaluation.

name: Pay-As-You-Go / Metered
what: Charge per call, per unit (message, minute, GB, token) with no commitment.
when: Usage varies widely and customers want to start small.
watch: Bill shock; publish calculators and alerts.

name: Tiered / Volume Pricing
what: The unit price drops as volume crosses thresholds.
watch: Graduated vs volume tiers confuse buyers, so state which one you use.

name: Committed Use / Prepaid Credits
what: Customers prepay or commit to spend in exchange for discounts.
watch: Expiring credits feel punitive.

name: Seat or Subscription Pricing with API Access
what: The API comes bundled with a SaaS subscription, priced per seat or account.
when: The API extends a product people already pay for.
watch: API access gated to top tiers frustrates integrators.
example: API available on Business plan and above

name: Outcome / Value-Based Pricing
what: Charge on the business result, such as a percentage of a payment or a successful verification.
when: The API's value tracks a measurable outcome.
watch: Disputes over what counted as a success.

name: Token / Compute-Based Pricing
what: Price on model tokens, compute seconds or credits consumed.
watch: Hard for buyers to forecast.

name: Revenue Share / Marketplace
what: Partners build on the API and split revenue through a marketplace or app store.
watch: Partner conflict and the platform competing with its own partners.
example: App marketplace with a 20% platform fee

name: Partner / Indirect Distribution
what: Sell API access through cloud marketplaces, resellers or aggregators.
watch: Margin and support handoffs.

name: Enterprise / Contact Sales
what: Custom contracts, volumes, SLAs and terms negotiated with sales.
watch: "Contact us" pricing hides cost from evaluators.

name: Published Pricing Page
what: Public, specific, machine-readable prices and limits per plan.
when: Always; buyers and agents both compare on it.
watch: Prices that drift from what billing charges.

name: Machine-Readable Plans
what: Plans, prices, limits and entitlements published as structured data an agent can read.
when: Agents and procurement tools need to compare APIs.
watch: Keeping it in sync with the pricing page.

name: Agent Payments / Pay-per-Call
what: Agents pay per request in-band, without a pre-existing account.
watch: Immature standards and fraud.
example: 402 Payment Required with a payment challenge

name: Billing and Invoicing APIs
what: Expose usage, invoices and spend to customers programmatically.
watch: Usage data that lags billing.

name: Spend Alerts and Caps
what: Customer-set budgets that notify or hard-stop at thresholds.
watch: Hard caps that break production unexpectedly.

name: Overage Policy
what: A defined behavior when quota is exceeded: block, throttle, or bill extra.
watch: Undocumented overage charges.

name: Eligibility and Access Requirements
what: Who may use the API: approval, KYC, region, partner status or business type.
watch: Opaque approval processes stall developers.

name: Service Level Agreement (SLA)
what: Contractual uptime, latency and support commitments with credits.
watch: SLAs without measurement or published status.

name: Support Tiers
what: Response-time commitments by plan (community, email, dedicated).
watch: Promising response times you cannot staff.

name: Terms of Service
what: The legal terms for using the API: acceptable use, liability, termination.
watch: Terms that forbid the use cases you market.

name: Privacy Policy and Data Processing
what: How personal data passing through the API is collected, processed and retained, plus DPAs.
watch: Policies that ignore API data flows.

name: Data Licensing
what: Explicit license on the data the API returns: open, attribution, commercial, or restricted.
when: Data APIs, open data and content APIs.
watch: Silence, which leaves reuse legally unclear.

name: API Definition Licensing
what: License the contract (OpenAPI, SDKs) separately from the service so others can reuse it.
watch: Unlicensed specs block forks and mirrors.
refs: Oracle v. Google context, API Commons

name: AI Usage Preferences
what: State whether content and data may be used to train or ground AI, in machine-readable form.
when: Content and data providers deciding on AI terms.
watch: Signals that are not enforced.
example: ai.txt, robots.txt AI agents, Content-Usage header
refs: IETF AI Preferences WG, apis.io AI Preferences

name: Compliance Attestations
what: Publish the certifications and frameworks the API meets.
watch: Badges without current reports.
example: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, HIPAA

name: Regulatory Alignment
what: Design to a sector's mandated API rules: open banking, healthcare interoperability, payments.
watch: Treating compliance as documentation instead of design.

name: Data Residency
what: Let customers pin data and processing to regions.
watch: Regional endpoints fragment discovery.

name: Deprecation Policy
what: A published commitment on notice periods and the support lifetime of versions.
when: Any API with paying or production consumers.
watch: Policies nobody follows.

name: Security Disclosure (security.txt)
what: Tell researchers how to report vulnerabilities.
watch: An unmonitored inbox.

name: Postman Collections
what: Runnable request collections that let developers try an API immediately.
watch: Collections that drift from the contract.

name: JSON-LD / Linked Data
what: Annotate payloads and pages with linked-data context so machines understand meaning.
when: Search engines, knowledge graphs and agents.
watch: Vocabulary choice and upkeep.

name: Spectral / Governance Rules
what: Codify the API style guide as lintable rules run in CI.
when: More than one team designs APIs.
watch: Rules nobody can explain get waived.

name: Vendor Extensions
what: x- properties that carry metadata the specification does not.
when: Gateways, codegen and docs need extra hints.
watch: Proprietary lock-in.

name: Public Source Repository
what: Contracts, SDKs and examples live in public version control with issues open.
when: Building trust and accepting fixes from consumers.
watch: Stale repos signal an abandoned API.

name: Agent Skills
what: Packaged instructions and scripts that teach an agent to use your API well.
when: Agents misuse an API without guidance.
watch: Skills that drift from the API.

name: Business Capabilities Map
what: Describe what the API lets a business accomplish, mapped to the operations behind it.
when: Buyers and agents search by outcome, not endpoint.
watch: Capability lists that do not tie to real operations.

name: API Estate / Portfolio
what: Manage many APIs across brands, acquisitions and teams as one governed estate.
when: Large companies with dozens of API products.
watch: Duplicate, inconsistent APIs across business units.
